facts.fact: One origin story credits Michel Ésper at the Club Deportivo Potosino in San Luis Potosí in the 1960s. He asked for beer with lime, salt and ice, and members started ordering 'Michel's limonada', which was shortened to 'michelada'.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelada (citing Los Angeles Times, 'Soul on Ice', 2003)

facts.fact: The other popular etymology reads 'michelada' as a mash-up of 'mi chela helada', meaning 'my ice-cold beer'. 'Chela' is Mexican slang for beer.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelada (citing Los Angeles Times 2003 and Texas Monthly 2014)

facts.fact: A chelada is the simple version: beer, lime and salt. A michelada adds spice and a juice or purée such as Clamato, tomato or hot sauce, though usage varies by region. Budweiser's 2008 'Chelada' was the first prepackaged michelada-style drink sold in the US.
Clamato in its modern form was launched by Duffy-Mott in 1966 as a Manhattan clam chowder-inspired tomato cocktail. Keurig Dr Pepper now owns it, and in Mexico it is a standard michelada mixer.

Red beer (light lager plus tomato juice) is an upper-Midwest staple, especially in Nebraska and Minnesota. It also goes by Red Eye, Red Rooster, Red Draw, Bloody Beer and Montana Mary, and some drinkers add a raw egg.
Red beer is typically a morning or early-afternoon drink. One theory ties it to canned tomato juice, which became widely available in the 1930s and '40s.

Wisconsin's tomato-and-beer ritual is the 'chaser' or 'snit', a short glass of beer served alongside a Bloody Mary. Bartenders outside Wisconsin and parts of Minnesota often don't know the custom, and Milwaukee bars pour Miller Lite, Schlitz or a pony of Miller.
facts.source: https://onmilwaukee.com/articles/milwaukee-og-bloody-mary-chaser (OnMilwaukee, 2022); https://www.insidehook.com/drinks/wisconsin-american-cocktail-drinking-capitol (InsideHook, 2020, dates the snit ritual to roughly the 1980s)

facts.fact: Milwaukee now has its own Michelada Fest at Zócalo Food Park in Walker's Point. The first was April 26, 2025, presented by Pilot Project Brewing with 15 competing bars, and the second was April 25, 2026.

recipes.name: Michelada (Dressed Up Mexican Beer)

ingredients.item: kosher or sea salt, for the rim
hot sauce such as Tabasco, Cholula or Valentina (optional, for michelada especial)
salty sauce such as soy sauce, Worcestershire or Maggi (optional)

steps: Spread salt on a small plate, rub the mug rim with the lime wedge, and dip the rim in the salt.
Basic version: add ice if using, pour in the lime juice, then the beer.
Michelada especial: add the optional seasonings to the salted mug, stir lightly, then pour in the beer.

recipes.name: Michelada con Camarones (Clamato michelada with shrimp)

ingredients.item: lime juice, plus extra for the rims
chile powder, for the rims and shrimp

steps: Pour lime juice onto one plate and chile powder onto another; dip the rims of four pint mugs in lime, then chile powder.
Dip the tops of the shrimp in chile powder and set aside.
Blend the Clamato, lime juice, orange juice, Worcestershire, pepper, salt, garlic and serrano until smooth.
Divide the mixture among the mugs, fill with ice, and top each with a lager.
Thread 6 shrimp onto each of 4 skewers and rest one across each mug.

recipes.name: Red Beer Deluxe (Midwest red beer)

ingredients.item: light lager (Busch Light, Coors Light or Grain Belt suggested; Miller Lite or Schlitz for a Milwaukee touch)

steps: Combine the beer, tomato juice and olive brine in a chilled mug.
Add the green olives and the salt.
Garnish with two dill pickle slices.
recipes.note: No published Wisconsin-specific red beer recipe was found. This upper-Midwest version from Punch is the closest reputable one. The light-lager-plus-tomato-juice base matches VinePair's and Chowhound's descriptions of the regional drink, and the Milwaukee beer substitution is my suggestion, not Punch's.

open_questions: Michelada Fest 2025 and 2026 winners were not named in any article found (Urban Milwaukee, OnMilwaukee, Milwaukee Record, WISN, CBS 58, Shepherd Express). Zócalo's Facebook or Instagram may have them.

Almost no Milwaukee venue publishes a michelada recipe, beer or garnish list. The garnish arrays for places are empty rather than guessed, and an illustrator should rely on the generic photo refs (Tasting Table super-garnished michelada, Clamato shrimp michelada).

No Milwaukee bar was found that lists 'red beer' or 'red eye' on a menu. In Wisconsin the tomato-and-beer custom shows up mainly as the Bloody Mary beer chaser (snit), which belongs to the Bloody Mary agents. Most taverns will pour a red beer on request, but none was verified.
Fiesta Café: current hours and michelada menu listing unverified (the site blocks fetching; last published hours are from 2019).
Camacho's Bar, El Señorial, Beto's Pizza: hours not found.
Zócalo tavern late-October hours not found. It is an outdoor park, so cold-weather hours may be shorter.
Banderas planned weekend breakfast with 'hangover helpers' (Aug 2025); whether it now opens before 4 PM on weekends is unconfirmed.
Birch's tomato martini is seasonal (returned Sept 2026); availability on Oct 24 unconfirmed.

Closed or changed (avoid): La Perla (734 S 5th St) closed July 2022; La Fuente (625 S 5th St) stopped regular restaurant service in 2017; Sobelman's Marquette location closed May 2023 (the 1900 W St Paul Ave original was still open as of Oct 2024); Electric Lime moved to 811 N Jefferson St, dinner only, no michelada listed; Café Corazón's site now lists only Riverwest and Brown Deer, and its drink menu shows a Bloody Maria but no michelada; Don Camarón (1234 S Cesar Chavez) is marked closed on Yelp; Micheladas Galán (2020 delivery-only michelada truck) status unknown.

Handoff for the Bloody agents: Pilot Project Brewing (1128 N 9th St) has a Sunday-only Bloody Mary bar (10 AM to 3 PM) with a Tajín rim option. Café Corazón has a $9 Bloody Maria. Fiesta Café has had a Southwest Bloody.
